item.title: Dimension Amplification for Tarski Fixed-Point Query Lower Bounds
item.description:
Filter match: keyword: query complexity

Authors: Boyu Liu, Zihe Wang

We prove that finding a fixed point of a monotone map on the nine-dimensional grid $[N]^9$ requires $Ω((\log N)^3)$ deterministic queries, even when the fixed point is unique and each query returns the entire function value. The proof gives a construction that raises the dimension from $d$ to $4d+1$, preserves uniqueness, and adds a logarithmic factor to the lower bound. Iteration gives $Ω((\log N)^{r+2})$ queries in dimension $(7\cdot4^r-1)/3$, for every fixed nonnegative integer $r$, with an implicit constant that may depend on $r$. Consequently, no finite logarithmic exponent bounds the query complexity in all fixed dimensions.

item.title: Recognizers for Graph-Encoding Languages
item.description:
Filter match: keyword: local computation

Authors: Anssi Yli-Jyrä

We introduce recurrent incidence automata (RIAs), a new automaton model motivated by a decomposition of certain two-stack visibly pushdown computations. The decomposition separates vertex-local finite-state computations from recurrent one-stack interfaces connecting consecutive vertices. The construction is motivated by a two-stack visibly pushdown encoding of arbitrary ordered graphs whose strings admit a unique factorization into center-foldable vertex-local factors and whose auxiliary stack is empty at every factor boundary. Folding each factor into a sequence of pair symbols yields a local interface transformation. An RIA consists of a finite-state unit that computes these transformations and a recurrent layer that composes them across consecutive factors. Rather than manipulating an internal pushdown store, RIAs externalize long-range stack memory into recurrent interfaces between local computations. We show that nondeterministic RIA languages are closed under union, intersection, concatenation, Kleene-*, and reversal. Deterministic RIAs are closed under Boolean operations, although emptiness remains undecidable.

item.title:
TR26-231 | Tarski Fixed Points in Quasi-FPT Queries |
Xi Chen,
Ruiquan Gao,
Yuhao Li,
Aviad Rubinstein,
Mihalis Yannakakis
item.description:
Filter match: keyword: query complexity

We study the query complexity of finding a Tarski fixed point over $[n]^k$. Previous work has left a large gap between $\smash{{\Omega}(\log^2 n)}$ and $\smash{\log^{O(k)}n}$. We show that both of the previous upper and lower bounds were far from tight: for every $k\geq 3$, $$ \Omega\left((\log n)^{\frac{1}{2}\lceil \log k\rceil}\right)\le \textrm{Tarski}(n,k)\le O\left(5^k (\log n)^{\lceil \log k\rceil}\right).$$ Succinctly, up to the fixed-parameter factor of $5^k$, the complexity is settled at $(\log n)^{\Theta(\log k )}$. In particular, we obtain the first super-polynomial query lower bound for this problem.

item.title: Cores Characterize the One-Pass Streaming Complexity of CSPs
item.description:
Filter match: keyword: streaming algorithm

Authors: Joshua Brakensiek, Aaron Putterman, Amatya Sharma, Santhoshini Velusamy

We study the one-pass streaming complexity of CSPs over a fixed finite relation $R$ under three natural objectives: $\textsf{SAT}(R)$, deciding whether all constraints can be satisfied; $\textsf{Min}$-$\textsf{CSP}(R)$, approximately minimizing the number of unsatisfied constraints; and $\textsf{Exact-CSP}(R)$, exactly computing the maximum number of satisfied constraints. Sharma and Velusamy (ESA 2026) characterized the streaming complexity of satisfiability for CSPs with literals using the non-redundancy parameter $\textsf{NRD}_n(R)$, which roughly measures the largest instance in which every constraint is independently necessary. For the most general setting without literals, they obtained the corresponding characterization for Boolean relations and showed obstacles to extending their techniques to larger domains. Kol, Paramonov, Saxena, and Yu (ITCS 2023) similarly characterized the streaming complexity of $\textsf{Exact-CSP}(R)$ for Boolean CSPs with literals in terms of the degree deg$(R)$ of the relation when written as a polynomial, while without literals, the corresponding result was known only for $\textsf{Max-Cut}$. For all three of the objectives we study, we give tight characterizations for unweighted CSP instances over arbitrary finite domains. The streaming algorithms we provide are deterministic, while the corresponding bounds are tight up to polylogarithmic factors, even against randomized algorithms. The central idea in all three results is a reduction of $R$ to its core, a canonical subrelation of $R$ which admits gadgets that allow for the hard-pinning (or fixing) of variables.

item.title: Symmetric Submodular Minimization from Comparisons
item.description:
Filter match: keyword: minimum cut

Authors: James Fox, David P. Woodruff

Given value-oracle access to a symmetric submodular function $f:2^V\to\mathbb{R}$ with $|V|=n$, a nontrivial minimizer can be found using $O(n^3)$ value queries. We study the weaker comparison model, in which a query on $S,T\subseteq V$ reveals only whether $f(S)$ is smaller than, equal to, or larger than $f(T)$. We give a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm that finds a nontrivial minimizer of any symmetric submodular function using $O(n^3)$ comparisons, matching the best-known deterministic value-oracle bound despite not knowing the function values. More generally, the same $O(n^3)$-comparison bound holds for minimization over the nonempty members of any downward-closed family. Our algorithm combines the minimum-capacity ordering recently introduced by Iwata and Konno with the contraction framework of Goemans and Soto. Applying this result to weighted graph cut functions resolves the main open question of Cohen-Addad et al., who gave an $\widetilde{O}(n^3)$-comparison algorithm that runs in exponential time and asked whether a weighted minimum cut can be found in polynomial time using comparisons. For graphs with $m$ edges of integer weight at most $B$, we also give a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm that finds a minimum cut using \[ \widetilde{O}\!\left(n^2+\min\!\left\{mB,\,nB^2\right\}\right) \] comparisons, improving on the $O(n^3)$ bound when $B$ is small. Finally, we show that every randomized algorithm that outputs a minimum cut with probability at least $2/3$ makes $Ω(n \log n)$ expected comparisons in the worst case. Under the stronger assumption that all edge weights are polynomially bounded integers, we obtain an $Ω(n \log \log n)$ expected comparison lower bound. These bounds contrast with the value-oracle model, where no $ω(n)$ lower bound is known even for deterministic algorithms.

item.title: Efficient Recovery of Latent Coordinate Structure from Sparse Observations of the Hypercube
item.description:
Filter match: keyword: minimum cut

Authors: Rares-Darius Buhai, Davide Mazzali, Weronika Wrzos-Kaminska

Recovering latent geometric structure from graph observations is a well-studied problem in statistical inference. Kapralov, Trevisan, and Wrzos-Kaminska (2026) introduced the problem of recovering the coordinate structure of the Boolean hypercube from a small random sample of its edges. More specifically, there are $n=2^d$ vertices, each corresponding to a distinct "feature" vector in $\{\pm 1\}^d$. Between each pair whose feature vectors are at Hamming distance one, an edge is observed independently with probability $p$. As long as the expected degree $pd$ is $\gtrsim \log d = \log \log n$, we give a polynomial-time algorithm that, given only the graph of observed edges, correctly recovers the entire feature vector of all but a vanishing fraction of vertices. This matches the information-theoretic guarantee of Kapralov, Trevisan, and Wrzos-Kaminska in polynomial rather than exponential time, resolving the algorithmic question left open by their work. Our algorithm combines a degree-$4$ sum-of-squares certificate for the structure of balanced near-minimum cuts with a rounding scheme originally developed for tensor decomposition by Ma, Shi, and Steurer (2016). The analysis relies on two novel ingredients: a sum-of-squares version of the Friedgut-Kalai-Naor theorem in Boolean Fourier analysis and a spectral concentration result for the observed subgraph of the hypercube. Finally, we provide a justification for why higher-degree sum-of-squares might be needed by showing a limitation of the basic SDP relaxation of this problem.

item.title: Faster Planar Graph Algorithms for Connectivity Problems via Meanders
item.description:
Filter match: keyword: connectivity

Authors: Susanna Caroppo, Giordano Da Lozzo, Giuseppe Di Battista, Jevgēnijs Vihrovs

In this paper, we refine the dynamic programming framework based on the sphere cut decomposition designed by Dorn, Penninkx, Bodlaender, and Fomin (ESA 2005) to obtain faster subexponential algorithms for connectivity problems on planar graphs. We investigate the relationship between these problems and meanders, which are simple closed planar loops that intersect a fixed line in a given number of points. By combining dynamic programming with techniques from meandric system analysis and the use of fast matrix multiplication by Dorn (ESA 2006), we obtain improved algorithms for planar connectivity problems. We show that the number of meanders on $2n$ crossings $M_n$ is $\mathcal O^*(12.806^n)$, which improves the previous upper bound of $\mathcal O^*(12.901^n)$ by Albert and Paterson (FPSAC 2004). This then gives the best-known classical upper bounds on the deterministic time complexity of several planar graph problems with polynomially-bounded weights, namely $\mathcal O(2^{5.543\sqrt n})$ for the Planar Travelling Salesman problem, $\mathcal O(2^{5.796\sqrt n})$ for Planar Longest Cycle/Path, $\mathcal O(2^{8.251\sqrt n})$ for Planar Connected Dominating Set and $\mathcal O(2^{8.037\sqrt n})$ for Planar Steiner Tree. Notably, this leads to the best-known deterministic complexity $\mathcal O(2^{5.543\sqrt{n}})$ for the Planar Hamiltonian Cycle problem.

item.title: Parallel Edge Ranking of Trees
item.description:
Filter match: keyword: sublinear

Authors: Jeff Giliberti, MohammadTaghi Hajiaghayi, Changki Yun

In this work, we prove that computing the edge ranking of a tree in parallel is P-Complete. An optimal tree edge ranking assigns positive integer ranks to the edges such that any two edges with the same rank are separated by an edge of higher rank, while minimizing the highest rank. Tree edge ranking abstracts several classical problems such as parallel assembly in manufacturing, minimum-height dendrograms, reversible pebble game and edge-query binary search on trees. Its parallel complexity remained open for over thirty years, since the seminal work of de la Torre, Greenlaw, and Sch{ä}ffer [SODA'93], and was listed as an open problem in the book Limits to Parallel Computation by Greenlaw, Hoover, and Ruzzo [1995]. We prove that deciding whether a tree has edge ranking at most $K$ is P-Complete, already for trees of diameter six. Our reduction is from NOR-CVP and simulates a greedy procedure underlying known sequential approaches. Despite ruling out NC algorithms, we prove that this hardness barrier can be bypassed in the well-known model of Massively Parallel Computation (MPC) with strongly sublinear local memory, showing that $O(\log n)$ MPC rounds suffice to solve the hard tree-edge ranking instances used to prove P-Completeness. Specifically, we present a deterministic MPC algorithm that computes an optimal edge ranking of an $n$-vertex tree of diameter $D$ in $O(\log D+\log\log n)$ rounds with $O(n^{3/4}D^{1/4})$ local memory. Our algorithm circumvents the linear-memory barrier by compressing the information required to produce a lexicographically minimal ranking from subtree merges. Overall, this result reinforces the strict separation between NC and what can be computed efficiently in MPC.

item.title: $Ω((\log n/\log\log n)^2)$ Lower Bounds for Dynamic Graph Problems
item.description:
Filter match: keyword: connectivity

Authors: Young Kun Ko

We prove an $Ω((\log n/\log\log n)^2)$ unconditional lower bound on the maximum of the query time and update time for dynamic data structures supporting reachability queries in $n$-node directed acyclic graphs under edge insertions. This improves the $\widetildeΩ(\log^{3/2} n)$ lower bound of Larsen and Yu [SICOMP 2025], and matches the strongest lower bound known for any dynamic problem. The same bound holds for incremental undirected shortest paths and subgraph connectivity. To prove it, we bring the recent framework of Ko [FOCS 2026], which gave this bound for Pătraşcu's multiphase problem with Inner Product, to the multiphase problem with Disjointness. Our main technical contribution is to show that verification in Ko's 2.5-round multiphase communication game makes a one-sided corruption bound suffice in place of discrepancy, which Disjointness lacks.

We prove an $\Omega((\log n/\log\log n)^2)$ unconditional lower bound on the maximum of the query time and update time for dynamic data structures supporting reachability queries in $n$-node directed acyclic graphs under edge insertions. item.title: TCS, AI, and the Adults in the Room
item.description:
Filter match: person: sepehr assadi

Guest Post by Clément Canonne, PDF version

When I was a kid, my parents looked in control. Even when bad things happened, they knew what to do, what to say, told us not to worry, did the things adults do to make things work out, and things did work out.

Now that I am less of a kid, I realize that they were not (always) in control. When bad things happened, they took responsibility to reclaim agency. They put on an adult face, figured out what to say, told us not to worry, and then silently did whatever they could so that things worked out. They just did their best, and we did not know, and we did not have to worry.

And now, for something completely different.

AI. We’re currently facing a rather obvious crisis, “what happens when a self-proclaimed unstoppable force meets a historically very slow-moving object.” I’m not going to detail what you probably all have witnessed and seen evolve over what feels like an eternity and the blink of an eye, but we need to reevaluate many things. Bad things are happening.1 We are not in control. We do not really know what to do. But, as Omer Reingold wrote so well,2 if you are a senior academic or industry researcher, snap out of it:

“Contemplating the end of your profession from the relative comfort of an established, tenured career is a privilege, and it comes with responsibilities. Senior academics are not merely individual researchers; we are stewards of our field, and we owe our junior colleagues active leadership rather than abandonment.”

Perhaps more bluntly, and less eloquently than Omer put it: we “senior academics” are supposed to be the adults. Complacency, doom-erism, and generally navel-gazing, while tempting, are unacceptable, counter-productive, and frankly unbecoming: we have a duty of care to our students, mentees, our community.

We need to put on an adult face, figure out what to say to them, tell them not to worry, and then silently do whatever we can so that things work out for them.

That’s not to say we should lie! It is, again, about taking responsibility, and coming up with a plan and solutions: letting others know that we are here for them, and that they can count on us. So I’ll outline some thoughts here about what to do now: mostly two. (1) We must find out what we want to fight for and preserve. (2) One concrete action to take.

What’s below is mostly targeted at “senior people,” but feel free to read on if you are junior – Ph.D., postdoc, untenured faculty or (good god!) born after The Dark Knight was released in theaters.

(1) We need to figure out what our values are, our justification, and we need to do it yesterday.

So let’s all take a break from freaking out about the latest longstanding conjecture whose resolution just appeared on the arXiv, and think about what it means to be doing Theoretical Computer Science, what our social mandate is, why we are doing what we are doing and why society has been paying us (quite well, actually) to do so.

  • Is it to create knowledge, investigate fundamental questions for the very sake of it?

  • Is is to disseminate knowledge, practical and/or abstract, to society?

  • Is it to equip students, undergraduate and postgraduate, with a specific set of skills, to view and navigate the world with a computational mindset?

  • Is it to solve problems relevant to society and to industry, with the bulk of our research being in some sense a “side quest” in support of this goal?

  • …

  • Is it to keep us at arms’ length, and prevent a bunch of people with an unhealthy knack for solving math puzzles from doing much worse things, like building an underground lair or starting a financial crisis?

Or is it something else entirely? Or a combination of all of the above? We may all have slightly different views on this, and I don’t have definite answers, but we should all be thinking about it (or, rather, we should all already have been thinking about it). Thankfully, we don’t have to start from nothing, because the giants whose shoulders we are camping on did give it some thought, and still are (see,  [@AhoJKKMPP96], and the response [@GoldreichW96] for a start3): but we must, starting from there, form our own opinions, decide what our values are, why we do what we do, and why society should give us a license to do so. We won’t know what to do, can’t figure out what to say, unless we know why we do what we do and what we stand for as a community.

Putting my money where my mouth is, here are some of my own views. 4

  1. We are meant to create knowledge, build theories, and new ways to look at things This involves many different aspects, among which “proving theorems” is at best the tip of the iceberg (unfortunately, as for icebergs, this is also usually the only one people notice). We should explore what “computation” means and could mean, driven by curiosity, yes, but also because it reveals new understanding which can shape the way we, and down the line many others, think. I see the concept of reduction between problems and the shift in thinking associated with it as one of the most beautiful and influential contributions of TCS: one which not only influenced (deeply) the theory of computation, algorithms, and complexity, but also one we teach our students, and might change the lens through which they view other aspects of their life.

  2. We are not mathematically-inclined tech consultants. As theoretical computer scientists, our reason d’être is not to solve problems from or for industry, or to only worry about current or near-future practical tasks they want to solve.5 This is not to say we shouldn’t think about these problems as a source of potentially interesting research questions. Interesting algorithmic questions can come out of anywhere, and industry has often happened to be a good source! But “you are not solving a practical problem” is not a valid criticism of TCS, much like “you are not building fridges” is not a damning indictment of thermodynamics.

  3. We are meant to create knowledge, but that means disseminating it. The license society gives us for our curiosity-driven endeavours and theory building comes with a price:6 we need to then explain this knowledge, communicate and teach it to our peers, our research community, our graduate students, and have it percolate through our teaching for it to reach as many people as possible. Knowledge creation without efforts towards exposition and dissemination is just a self-centered endeavour, with no benefit to the research community or society, and no place in academia.

And if you’re wondering where to have these discussions, and how to be able to debate and exchange ideas in a fragmented world, I have good news (or at least a suggestion): StackExchange! CSTheory.SE (https://cstheory.stackexchange.com/) exists; it can be used; let’s use it!

That was the first point. The second one, equally important: what can we do to make things work for our students, postdocs, and the new generation? Again, I don’t have answers, just one big suggestion: let’s shield them during this chaotic transition.

(2) Look at whatever grant you have, or can apply for, put funding together, call every possible philanthropist or funding body you can, be creative: let’s offer as many 2-, 3-, 4-year fellowships, postdoc, or early-career researchers positions as possible for juniors to weather the storm.

Let me be clear: if you are tenured (or have a similarly stable position), now is not the time for hand-wringing. But a 3-year postdoc position which includes part-time teaching (assuming, as I do, that great teaching and exposition will always be in demand) or some side industry experience? This could make the difference between a promising researcher leaving the field, or managing to make it through and adapt to the changes our discipline is going through. A small endowment from some startup or industry? This could tip the scales and provide stability just for the few months a PhD student needs before landing a job they want. So now is the time to try our very best, and, without publicly lamenting the end of our field (or, worse, rejoicing in it), to silently do whatever we can to so that things work out for the new generation.

And of course, do take me up on it. I’ll be trying, too (if I don’t, you know where to find me. There’s probably a very short flight from where you are to Sydney, and my office is always open.)

Thanks to Sepehr Assadi, Sasho Nikolov, and Omer Reingold for very helpful feedback on earlier versions of this post.

  1. Some good ones, too. ↩

  2. If you haven’t, go read his post on the Theory Dish: https://theorydish.blog/2026/09/29/speeding-up-the-process-of-mourning/. ↩

  3. And a blog post by Lance Fortnow providing some context and perspective here: https://blog.computationalcomplexity.org/2016/06/karp-v-wigderson-20-years-later.html. ↩

  4. As I said, I don’t have definite answers: if you threw a rock in the general direction of the TCS community, you’d likely hit someone (i) with slightly different opinions, (ii) looking furious about a recent bump on their head. ↩

  5. There is a counterpart, though: we should not “claim practical relevance” if there is none. We are not beholden to solving industry questions, but if we claim to do so it has to be true. Cake, eating, having it too! ↩

  6. It’s a small price, but one we tend not to focus on unfortunately. For several reasons, among which that it’s typically less explicitly asked of us, and while it does take a lot of time it comes with few incentives. ↩

By Hung Le

item.title:
TR26-248 | Breaking the Parity Barrier for Constant-Depth Circuits |
Nikolai Chukhin
item.description:
Filter match: keyword: sparsification

A constant-depth circuit consists of AND and OR gates of unbounded fan-in, arranged in a constant number of layers, that read the input literals; for example, a depth-three circuit is an OR of CNFs or an AND of DNFs. The classical lower bound of Håstad (1989) states that every depth-$d$ circuit computing the parity function has $2^{\Omega(n^{1/(d-1)})}$ gates. This parity barrier stood for decades: no explicit function was known to require depth-$d$ circuits of size $2^{\omega(n^{1/(d-1)})}$ for any constant $d$. OpenAI (2026) recently announced that they broke this barrier for depth-three circuits: they gave an explicit function in P that requires OR-AND-OR circuits of size $2^{\omega(\sqrt{n})}$. In this paper, we break the parity barrier at every constant depth with a simpler function. We prove that for every fixed $d \ge 3$, every depth-$d$ circuit computing the trilinear function $\sum_{i,j} a_{i+j} x_i y_j \bmod 2$ for $x,y \in \{0,1\}^n$ and $a \in \{0,1\}^{2n-1}$, requires $2^{\Omega((n\log n/\log\log n)^{1/(d-1)})}$ gates. Our proof combines the restriction lemma of OpenAI, for which we give a short new proof, with Håstad's switching lemma and the sparsification lemma of Calabro, Impagliazzo, and Paturi (2006).

item.title: Simultaneous Competitive and Regret Guarantees for TCP Acknowledgment
item.description:
Filter match: keyword: sublinear

Authors: Tsubasa Harada, Yasushi Kawase, Hanna Sumita

We study simultaneous competitive and regret guarantees for TCP acknowledgment. Each acknowledgment serves all pending packets, and the objective is to minimize the total acknowledgment and waiting costs. It is well known that no deterministic online algorithm achieves a competitive ratio better than $2$. Given $k$ randomized online experts and $0<\varepsilon<1$, we construct a randomized online algorithm whose realized total cost is always at most $(2+\varepsilon)$ times the offline optimal cost $\mathrm{OPT}$ and whose expected regret against the expert with the smallest realized cost is $O(\sqrt{\mathrm{OPT}\log(k+1)}+\log(1/\varepsilon))$. The algorithm requires no advance knowledge of the number of packets or $\mathrm{OPT}$. Our algorithm controls switching costs between experts and uses the gap between the permitted competitive bound and its current cost to determine when to learn. We also prove lower bounds showing that, for $k\ge 2$, this regret bound is asymptotically optimal in $\mathrm{OPT}$, $k$, and $\varepsilon$, and that $\varepsilon>0$ is necessary for sublinear regret.

item.title: Breaking Two Barriers for Dynamic Planar Reachability
item.description:
Filter match: keyword: sparsification

Authors: Adam Karczmarz, Michał Włodarczyk

We consider the reachability problem in fully dynamic directed planar graphs: the graph undergoes edge updates (insertions and deletions) and we receive queries asking if one vertex is reachable from another. The current-best online algorithm for dynamic planar reachability spends worst-case time $\widetilde{O}(n^{2/3})$ per query/update [Subramanian, ESA '93]. This can be improved to $\widetilde{O}(n^{1/2})$ in the offline setting or when the embedding is fixed [Diks and Sankowski, ESA '07]. Our contribution is twofold: 1. We present the first algorithm that breaks the square-root barrier for dynamic planar reachability in the offline setting, obtaining time ${O}(n^{0.49})$ per query/update. This shows that the problem is easier than answering distance queries in a dynamic undirected planar graph, for which a conditional lower bound of $n^{1/2 - o(1)}$ is known [Abboud and Dahlgaard, FOCS '16]. Notably, this lower bound applies to both online and offline algorithms. 2. Second, in the general online setting we design a randomized data structure with amortized update and query time ${O}(n^{0.664})$. This is the first improvement upon the exponent $2/3$ in over three decades. The main engine behind our theorems is a new sparsification framework aimed at maintaining information about reachability. Specifically, we study digraphs through the lens of VC dimensionality of certain set systems. First, we design sparse reachability emulators for planar digraphs that preserve the VC dimension. Second, we utilize orderings with a low ``stabbing number'' [Chazelle and Welzl, Discrete Comput. Geom. '89] to compute subquadratic reachability emulators in subquadratic time whenever the VC dimension is bounded.
